analysis.one_liner: Makes it a crime for executives to hide known serious dangers from their products or services, and protects whistleblowers who speak up.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made it a crime for executives to sit on known product dangers, died in the House Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors and never reached a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime — punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine — for a company or its responsible executives to knowingly sit on knowledge that their product, service, or business practice poses a serious danger of death or serious injury. Once an executive actually knew of such a danger, the company would have 24 hours to tell the relevant federal agency, 15 days to follow up in writing, and a duty to warn exposed employees and other identifiable people who could be hurt. It would also have protected whistleblowers: workers who report these dangers could not be fired or demoted for it, could win back pay and reinstatement in court, and companies could not force them into arbitration or make them sign away these rights. The company could not pay an executive's fine for him. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the congressional session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and workers. Anyone who buys a product, uses a service, or works around equipment would learn within hours or days — instead of after an injury or lawsuit — when a company knows its product can kill or seriously hurt someone. Workers who know about a danger and report it would get enforceable legal protection: their job back, back pay, attorney's fees, and the right to take the case to a jury instead of private arbitration. The threat of personal criminal liability and prison time is aimed squarely at the executives who today can let a danger stay hidden while their company absorbs any fine.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years in prison and a fine, for a company or its responsible officers to knowingly sit on knowledge of a serious danger from their product, service, or business practice.

It sets hard deadlines: verbal notice to the relevant federal agency within 24 hours, written notice within 15 days, written warnings to exposed employees as soon as practicable, and notice to other identifiable people who may be exposed.
It bars the company from paying an executive's criminal fine — the penalty comes out of the officer's own pocket, not the corporation's.
It protects whistleblowers: workers who report dangers cannot be fired or demoted for it, and can win reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees through the Labor Department or federal court.

Those whistleblower rights cannot be waived, and companies cannot force workers into predispute arbitration over these claims — a common fine print practice that otherwise pushes such disputes out of court.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses whose products or services enter interstate commerce — essentially any company in America — and specifically the executives responsible for them. They would face a hard 24-hour reporting clock, a duty to warn employees and the public, and criminal fines and up to five years in prison for knowingly concealing a serious danger, with the fine payable only from the executive's own assets, not the company's. They would also lose the ability to bury whistleblower retaliation claims in arbitration.

drawbacks.text: The 24-hour deadline to report a 'serious danger' to a federal agency is tight, and businesses argued in similar debates that fast-moving judgments about what counts as a serious risk could expose executives to criminal charges for honest mistakes in assessing danger.

The bill reaches virtually any business whose products or services cross state lines, so companies across the economy would face new federal criminal exposure and compliance costs for disclosure, an expense that could be passed on in prices.

The bill bars companies from forcing these whistleblower disputes into predispute arbitration, which employers generally prefer as a faster, private, lower-cost way to resolve claims; companies would have to litigate them in court instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: faster disclosure of product and workplace dangers and legal protection for the employees who speak up, which could prevent injuries the current patchwork of agency-specific rules misses. The costs and design concerns are also real: a 24-hour federal reporting clock applied across every industry could push companies toward over-reporting out of caution, tying up regulators; "serious danger" is defined broadly enough that officers could face prison time over judgment calls about how imminent or severe a risk is; and imposing personal criminal liability on executives is a significant expansion of criminal law that opponents would argue could chill legitimate business decisions. On balance, the protections for consumers and workers are substantial, but the bill was never debated or refined in committee, so questions about its scope and workability were never answered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 2022, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and that is the last thing that ever happened to it — the session ran out with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on November 29, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and their executives are better off, because no law now requires them to disclose serious product dangers on a fixed clock or face criminal penalties, and workers still lack these specific whistleblower protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations and executives who avoided the duty

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition was recorded, but the bill's support was one Democratic member with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill imposed a 24-hour federal reporting duty and criminal liability (fines, up to 5 years' imprisonment) on companies and their officers who know of a serious product danger and fail to disclose it, plus whistleblower protections workers could enforce in court. Companies currently face no such uniform criminal duty to warn, so this would have closed a gap they benefit from.

Executives with authority over a dangerous product would face personal criminal liability — prison time and fines that the company is expressly barred from paying for them. Today, corporate fines are typically absorbed by the company and shareholders.

industries.industry: Arbitration industry and employers using predispute arbitration
industries.note: The bill declared predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for these whistleblower claims, keeping such disputes in court with a jury trial rather than private arbitration. This is the provision employers most commonly rely on to keep employment disputes out of the courts.
